markdownRemark.html:
This is part of a series about color that grew out of a loose end in my Exposure vs Brightness article. In What an RGB number actually means I learned that an RGB number is an instruction, not a color: a color space says which red, green and blue you mean. Its primaries form a triangle on a horseshoe-shaped map of visible color, and no number of bits gets you out of that triangle.

That article ended with a question I couldn’t stop thinking about. Why is the map that shape? And why three lights, anyway? Here is what I wanted to know:

  • Why only three primaries? Would five fix it?
  • Why can’t a primary sit right on the corner?
  • Where does the horseshoe come from? Why is that the limit, not bigger or smaller?

The color series: 1. What an RGB number actually means · 2. Where the horseshoe comes from (you are here) · 3. HSL and HSV: RGB with different knobs · 4. Lab: numbers that match what you see · 5. Why gradients go muddy

Disclaimer: This one is mostly theory, and I haven’t measured any of it myself. Claude explained it to me, and I recomputed the numbers in code to be safe. I’m still a beginner doing this to get better at game photography and to grow my Instagram channel, so I accept that I may have gotten something wrong along the way. If I did, I’d love a correction in the comments.

Key takeaways:

  • More primaries add reach and redundancy, not a dimension. The signal stays three numbers; a five-primary screen turns them into five drive values internally.
  • Three is the default because the eye has three cone types, and each reports a single number. Color, as a sensation, is a point in 3D.
  • The horseshoe is measured, not chosen. It is what you get by sweeping one wavelength of light across the spectrum. It is the gamut of a display with one primary for every wavelength.
  • Nothing real can sit outside it. To go beyond the edge you would need a light purer than a single wavelength, which means negative power somewhere.
  • The shape depends on the chart. The physics fixes the topology; the coordinate system sets the outline.

Why only three primaries? Would five fix it?

Yes, more primaries extend the gamut. Five primaries make a pentagon on the map instead of a triangle, and the more primaries you add along the curved edge, the closer you get to the whole horseshoe. Here is what that looks like. I put the first three on the edge of the horseshoe, near where BT.2020’s sit (465, 530 and 630 nm), and each new one goes wherever it adds the most area:

Interactive illustration (primaries-count). Open this article on antondanshin.com to try it.

Three well-placed single-wavelength lights cover about 65% of the horseshoe’s area on this chart (BT.2020 gets 64%, sRGB 34%). Add one at 505 nm, a cyan-green, and it jumps to 82%. Five primaries get you to 86%, eight to 96%, twelve to 99%. These are areas on the xy chart, which stretches the greens a lot, so don’t read them as “how much we notice”. More on that at the end.

This has been tried:

  • Sharp sold TVs with an extra yellow subpixel from 2010 (Quattron). Whether it gave the TV a real fourth primary was disputed: the Wikipedia article cites researchers who argued the backlight itself has no fourth primary to drive it.
  • Cinema projectors with six laser primaries exist (Christie’s, for example). They use two sets of red, green and blue, mostly to get 3D working with glasses, not to widen the gamut.
  • In printing, “extended gamut” adds orange, green and violet inks to CMYK (FESPA explains).

What a fifth light does, in math

Light adds up. If a screen has primaries with cone responses LMS(p₁), LMS(p₂), and so on, then any color it makes is

LMS = Σ aᵢ · LMS(primaryᵢ), aᵢ ≥ 0

where aᵢ is how much of each light you turn on. The LMS on the left is three numbers, so this is three equations.

  • Three primaries: three unknowns, three equations, one solution. It only works if every aᵢ comes out as zero or more, and that constraint is the triangle wall from What an RGB number actually means.
  • Five primaries: five unknowns, three equations. There are infinitely many mixes that give the same color, so the screen has to pick one (the most power-efficient, say). The reachable set is a bigger convex shape.

A fifth primary adds reach and redundancy, not a dimension. The signal stays three numbers, and a multi-primary TV works out the five drive values inside.

Why it never took over

I asked Claude why every screen is still three-primary, and this is what I got back. The first is my reading of the numbers above, I have no source for the second, and the last two have sources.

  1. Diminishing returns. Modern narrow-band emitters (lasers, quantum dots) already put three primaries near the edge. BT.2020’s primaries are single wavelengths, and that triangle already covers 64% in the numbers above. What is left is mostly the cyan-greens.
  2. More subpixels means smaller subpixels, so less light gets through. Claude explained this; I have no source for it.
  3. Content is made for three primaries. Standards like sRGB, P3 and BT.2020 all describe three-primary targets, so extra primaries need work in the display to convert.
  4. People disagree at the edges. Very pure primaries make person-to-person differences in cone sensitivity more visible, an effect called observer metamerism (RIT writes about it for multi-primary cinema).

Pro Tip: For my own work none of this changes anything. The ceiling that matters is the gamut of my screen (P3) and of where I post (Instagram is effectively sRGB for most viewers), not the three-primary limit.

Why three? Why can’t a primary sit on the corner?

Three primaries is the default because the eye has three cone types, called L, M and S (long, medium and short wavelengths). Each cone type reports one number: how much light it caught, weighted by wavelength. Color as a sensation is therefore a point in 3D, three primaries are the minimum to span it, and every image format stores three channels.

Here are the cone sensitivities, scaled so each type’s peak is 1 (the data is Stockman and Sharpe’s 2° cone fundamentals from CVRL):

Interactive illustration (cone-sensitivities). Open this article on antondanshin.com to try it.

Look at how much the L and M curves overlap. On my 5 nm table, at 550 nm the L cone responds at 94% and the M cone at 98% of their peaks. Both are above 90% from 545 to 560 nm. No real light stimulates only one cone type. If you could, you would get a color more saturated than anything in the horseshoe, but light always wakes up its neighbors.

That is why even a screen with perfect single-wavelength primaries can’t sit on a “pure L” or “pure M” corner. The curve of the horseshoe is that overlap made visible.

Where does the horseshoe come from?

The horseshoe isn’t a limit someone chose. It is measured, and it follows from a short argument:

  1. Any real light is a spectrum: some non-negative power at each wavelength. So every light is a non-negative sum of single-wavelength lights.
  2. The cones respond linearly: the response to a light is the sum of the responses to its wavelengths. So every light’s response is a non-negative combination of single-wavelength responses.
  3. Sweep one pure wavelength from 380 to 700 nm and plot where it lands. It traces a curve, the curved edge of the horseshoe. (The name for it is the spectral locus.)
  4. Every non-negative mix of points on that curve lies inside the shape it encloses, so all real colors fill the region.

Slide through the wavelengths and watch it get drawn. The bars show how strongly each cone type responds:

Interactive illustration (draw-the-horseshoe). Open this article on antondanshin.com to try it.

So the horseshoe is the gamut of a display with infinitely many primaries, one for every wavelength. That ties straight back to the first question:

  • Why not bigger? Outside would need a light purer than a single wavelength, meaning negative power at some wavelengths.
  • Why not smaller? Every point inside can be made by some physical mix.

Why that particular shape

  • From 700 nm down to about 570 nm (red through yellow), the S cones hardly respond. At 560 nm they respond at 0.1%. Only L and M change, and two quantities mixing give a straight line. I checked my table: from 570 to 700 nm the edge deviates from a straight line by less than 0.0001. That is the nearly straight edge on the right.
  • Around 500 nm (cyan-green) the S cones start to matter (12% at 500 nm, 3% at 520) and the curve bends sharply. The curve’s far-left point is at 505 nm (x 0.0039), and its top is at 520 nm (x 0.0743, y 0.8338). This is the region every display triangle misses the most.
  • From 500 down to 380 nm the S cones dominate, heading into blue-violet.
  • The flat bottom edge, the line of purples. No single wavelength makes magenta or purple. They exist only as mixes of the two ends of the spectrum, and mixing two points gives a straight line between them.
For nerds: where the data came from

This part is Claude’s explanation, checked against the Wikipedia article on CIE 1931.

In the late 1920s, Wright and Guild ran color-matching experiments with about 17 observers in total (Wright 10, Guild 7). Observers matched a pure test wavelength by adjusting three primary lights. For many wavelengths no match was possible, so a primary had to be added to the test side instead. That is the negative coefficient from the twist in What an RGB number actually means, observed in a lab. The CIE standardized the averaged result in 1931 as the “standard observer”, so it is an average and individuals deviate from it a little.

The shape depends on the chart

Everything on the map so far uses the CIE 1931 xy coordinates: x = X / (X + Y + Z) and y = Y / (X + Y + Z). Dividing by the sum removes brightness, and the transform keeps straight lines straight, which is why gamuts stay triangles. But it is not perceptually uniform. The huge green area is partly an artifact of the math, not a sign that we see lots of greens.

There is a later chart from 1976 with coordinates u′ = 4x / (−2x + 12y + 3) and v′ = 9y / (−2x + 12y + 3), designed so equal distances look more equal (it is the chart the CIE recommends for light sources, but it is still not perfectly uniform; see their technical note). Slide between the two and watch the same colors change shape:

Interactive illustration (xy-to-uv). Open this article on antondanshin.com to try it.

Same physics, different picture. The sRGB triangle covers about the same share in both charts (34% and 33%), but the wide spaces don’t: Display P3 goes from 46% to 42%, and BT.2020 from 64% to 57%. When you read “covers X% of visible colors” on a spec sheet, it matters which chart they used.

What I took away

The horseshoe isn’t a mystery shape. It is what you get from infinitely many primaries, one for every wavelength, and every real screen’s triangle (or pentagon) sits inside it. Three primaries are enough because the eye has three cone types, and the corners are out of reach because those cones overlap.

If you want to poke at it yourself, there is a small page with two tools: a gamut explorer (hover anywhere on the map and it tells you which color spaces can show that point) and a playground where you drag your own primaries around and watch how much of visible color they cover.

The map also answers a question I had put off. Every editor has sliders called hue, saturation and lightness, and I realized I couldn’t say what they measure. They don’t sit on this map at all: they are another way of labeling the same three RGB numbers. That is HSL and HSV: RGB with different knobs, and after it comes the color system that was built to sit on this map and match the eye.

Did I get something wrong, or do you think about this differently? The comments are open.
